title: Eggnog
summary: Thick, nutmeg-scented cooked egg custard drink, gently heated for safety and served cold.

ingredients.note: freshly grated if possible, plus extra to serve
or 60–90 ml (¼–⅓ cup) dark rum or brandy

steps: Whisk the egg yolks and erythritol in a bowl until pale and thick.
Heat the milk, cream, nutmeg, cinnamon and salt in a pan until steaming.
Pour the hot milk into the yolks in a thin stream, whisking all the time, then return everything to the pan.
Cook over low heat, stirring constantly with a spatula, until the mixture thickens slightly and reaches 71 °C (160 °F) on a thermometer. Do not let it boil or it will curdle.
Strain into a jug, stir in the vanilla and rum extract (or spirit), cool, then refrigerate at least 3 hours.
Whisk before serving and grate a little nutmeg over each glass.
dairy_free_notes: With almond milk and coconut cream the eggnog is a little thinner and tastes of coconut; nutmeg and rum carry it well.
tips: Erythritol can crystallise in the cold drink; allulose or a powdered sweetener stays dissolved.

origin.history: Eggnog descends from British posset, a medieval drink of hot milk curdled with wine or ale and sometimes thickened with eggs. In the American colonies, where milk, eggs and rum were plentiful, a cold egg-and-milk punch made with rum became a holiday favourite, and the name eggnog was in use by the eighteenth century. The origin of the word nog itself is uncertain.
